newsitem.title: USA: Cohen says US unsure about North Korean manoeuvres. [CORRECTED 08:10 GMT 13/4]
newsitem.headline: Cohen says US unsure about North Korean manoeuvres. [CORRECTED 08:10 GMT 13/4]

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen said on Friday the United States was puzzled by recent North Korean military manoeuvres and warned that tension over a hunger crisis there could spark a new Korean war "virtually without notice."

Speaking to reporters as he returned from South Korea, Cohen said that while the North's tank and troop movements did not appear threatening, they could be aimed at quashing unrest among civilians who are reported to be suffering from near-famine conditions.

He said the United States and South Korea hoped high-level North Korean defector Hwang Jang-yop, temporarily in the Philippines, will go to South Korea soon and provide insight into the state of mind of Pyongyang's military and government.

"There are a variety of reasons why they (North Korean forces) may have done this," including routine training, he said of the manoeuvres. "It may be to send a signal to any rebellious citizens. We just simply don't have any access into their mind-set. Maybe the defector will give us an insight.

"This is a very dangerous area that could erupt virtually without notice. They have a lot of chemical weapons. They have lots of Scuds (missiles)," Cohen told reporters flying home with him from Osan Air Base in South Korea at the end of a week-long trip to Japan and Korea.

"They (the North) could do some horrific damage in a short time," he said. "They would be devastated in return, but you're dealing with a regime that doesn't always act in a rational fashion so you have to be very cautious in dealings with them."

He spoke a day after visiting the demilitarized zone between the two Koreas only an hour after warning shots were exchanged by North and South Korean troops in one of hundreds of such incidents since the 1950-53 Korean War ended.
Separately, a U.S. senator just back from North Korea said North Koreans "were in a state of total mobilisation" during the recent visit by his congressional delegation.

"Every moving vehicle had to have camouflage on it" and North Korean airplanes were made to fly low "so as to give their people the right feel for war and what attack is all about," Republican Pete Domenici told a news conference.

The New Mexico (corrects from Arizona) senator said these manuevers, coupled with statements by North Korean officials that the military may not allow them to join four-party peace talks with the United States, South Korea and China, "leads me to believe they are having some very serious internal problems."
Cohen said earlier on Friday as he departed Osan that large-scale food aid to North Korea was highly unlikely until Pyongyang began dismantling its powerful military machine threatening the South.
"I doubt very much whether there will be massive assistance without some kind of reciprocal action on the part of the North Koreans," he told a news conference.

Cohen made clear the international community would not feed a hungry nation whose government was pouring scarce resources into a military geared for war and armed with chemical weapons and long-range missiles.

Aboard his aircraft later, he reiterated that Washington had no intention of using food aid as a bargaining chip with any starving country, but he stressed that it would move very cautiously with South Korea and Japan in providing such aid.

North Korea has said it will respond next Wednesday to a proposal for four-country peace talks, also including China, aimed at replacing a truce that ended the Korean War. But it has demanded substantial food aid in the past as the price for agreeing to sit at the peace table.

South Korea and the United States say aid can be discussed in the talks. In the meantime they have chipped in with relatively modest contributions to a World Food Programme appeal for 200,000 tons of food, well short of what is needed to stave off famine after two consecutive years of floods.
Asked about more aid, Cohen said: "Much will depend on what kind of progress is made as far as peace talks is concerned."
